_comment: KERB PARKING SPACES (ADR-0439): how the road model lays parking spaces along a street's kerb.
WHICH streets park, and how wide the parking band along each kerb is, is the road class's `parking`
(assets/data/road_classes.json; today only the local street: 2.5 m of its 6 m lane each way). This file says how
that band is cut into spaces. The road model reads it once (road_model.h kerbParkingRules) and states the spaces
(RoadModel::kerbRuns); everything else asks the model. There is no copy of these numbers in C++, and a missing or
unreadable file means no street has a space (the log says so).
space_length        metres of kerb one space takes, measured along the street's centre line. One car parked
parallel to the kerb, with room to pull in and out.
clear_of_stop_line  metres kept empty between a junction arm's stop line and the nearest space, on both kerbs
of the street. The stop line already stands back from the junction's area (ADR-0428), so
this also keeps spaces off the crosswalk and out of the way of turning traffic.
A street's end where it only carries on as another street (no junction), or a dead end, needs no clearance.
Where a street states the stretch buildings may front (the road file's lots_range), spaces keep to that stretch.
WHY THE NUMBERS. 7 m is the spacing the city sim has laid its kerbside bays at since it first parked cars, and
it fits every car, van and goods vehicle of the fleets (the longest, the goods van, is 6.7 m; a bus is 11.5 m
and does not park at a kerb). Real parallel spaces are 6.0 m (UK) to 6.7 m (US, 22 ft). 10 m is the UK Highway
Code's rule 243 (do not park within 10 metres of a junction); US states use 20 ft from a crosswalk and 30 ft
from a stop sign or signal, which is about the same once the stop line's own set-back is counted. The rule's
number and these lengths are quoted from memory, not checked against the texts. Both numbers are starting
values, marked [~]: tune them here.
